analysis.one_liner: Opens the Arctic Refuge and offshore waters to oil drilling, approves Keystone XL, and halts federal greenhouse gas rules.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: introduced in February 2013 with 23 Republican cosponsors, it was referred to the Senate Energy Committee and sat there until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have directed the Interior Department to sell oil and gas leases across most of the outer continental shelf, opened the coastal plain of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge to drilling for the first time, and declared the Keystone XL pipeline approved without a presidential permit. It would have also barred federal agencies from enforcing any carbon or greenhouse gas limits until China, India, and Russia adopted matching rules, stripped the president's power to create national monuments without Congress, and cut off federal payment of legal fees for environmental groups that challenge energy projects. It received no committee action and died when the 113th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas companies would gain new lease sales offshore and in the Arctic Refuge, 20-day deadlines on drilling permits, and a shortened, restricted court review process that limits challenges to their projects. TransCanada would get its Keystone XL pipeline deemed federally approved. The bill also restores long-term oyster farming permits for Drakes Bay Oyster Company in California and conveys land to two Alaska Native corporations.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Oil and gas companies and pipeline builders

how_it_helps.text: Requires Interior to hold lease sales every 270 days in any offshore planning area with commercial interest, approves drilling permits within 20 days, and declares the 2010-2015 offshore leasing plan final without further environmental review.

Repeals the ban on drilling in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge's coastal plain, orders a competitive leasing program there, and deems a 1987 environmental study sufficient review for the first lease sale.
Declares no presidential permit needed for the Keystone XL border pipeline, deems the 2011 State Department environmental review complete, and limits court challenges to a single appeals court.

Prohibits any federal agency from implementing or enforcing greenhouse gas emission reductions until the heads of EPA, the Energy Information Administration, and Commerce certify that China, India, and Russia have adopted substantially similar measures.
Requires Congress to approve any future national monument designations, ending the president's unilateral authority under the Antiquities Act.

Bars federal payment of legal fees to environmental groups whose lawsuits block energy, mining, timber, or grazing access, or eliminate jobs, and channels all challenges to energy projects into the D.C. federal courts on a 60-day filing deadline.

analysis.who_pays: The public bears the environmental and health costs of expanded fossil fuel development: offshore and Arctic Refuge drilling, a pipeline deemed approved without further review, and the rollback of greenhouse gas limits. Communities near drilling, coastal states that lose revenue shares to the federal treasury, and environmental and public-interest groups that could no longer recover legal fees would all pay a price.
analysis.who_pays_short: The public, coastal communities, and environmental groups

drawbacks.text: It would nullify existing U.S. greenhouse gas regulations until China, India, and Russia adopted matching rules — a certification that those agencies would be unlikely to make, effectively suspending U.S. climate rules indefinitely.

It opens the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge's coastal plain to drilling, deemming a 1987 environmental study adequate and limiting the government's own authority to close areas, with court review presumed correct unless a challenger proves otherwise by clear and convincing evidence.

It would forbid considering climate change impacts when protecting species under the Endangered Species Act and bar water project restrictions in California's Central Valley below historical maximum allocations.

Supporters' own cost: even the bill acknowledges environmental risk by writing in a 'no significant adverse effect' standard, seasonal drilling limits, a 12.5% minimum royalty, and reclamation duties — protections the bill itself concedes are necessary for Arctic development.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gains go overwhelmingly to oil and gas producers and pipeline companies: new lease sales, faster permits, a pre-approved pipeline, and narrowed court access. The bill does include real safeguards on Arctic drilling and sends 90% of new lease revenues to the Treasury, but the centerpiece provisions — suspending U.S. climate rules, pre-approving Keystone XL, opening the Refuge, and cutting off environmental groups' legal fees — shift costs onto the public in the form of emissions, habitat loss, and reduced ability to challenge federal energy decisions. On balance the bill's benefits flow to one concentrated industry while its costs are spread across everyone else.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, which never took it up, so it expired when the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: Senator David Vitter introduced the bill on February 27, 2013, with 23 Republican cosponsors and no Democratic support.
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources the same day; that was its last action.
The committee never held a hearing or markup, and the bill never reached the Senate floor or received a vote before the Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, existing offshore leasing plans, the Arctic Refuge drilling ban, federal greenhouse gas rules, and presidential monument authority all remained in place — outcomes the bill's own cosponsors were not able to change. Oil and gas companies did not gain the access the bill promised them.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Existing environmental and climate protections stayed in place

sides.party_line_note: Every one of the bill's 24 Senate supporters was a Republican, and with no Democratic cosponsor the bill received no committee action before the Congress ended.

industries.note: Mandated offshore lease sales, Arctic Refuge leasing, 20-day drilling permits, and restricted court review expand drilling access at public environmental expense. The bill's revenue and safeguard provisions do not offset the core transfer of access and reduced oversight to the industry.
Declares the Keystone XL border pipeline federally approved without a presidential permit and limits legal challenges to one appeals court, granting the company a permit route no other applicant has.

Suspends all federal greenhouse gas regulations until China, India, and Russia adopt matching rules, relieving carbon-intensive generators of compliance costs while the public bears the resulting emissions.

Bars federal payment of their legal fees in cases that block energy, timber, grazing, or water access, and channels all energy project challenges into one court on a 60-day deadline — raising the cost of public-interest litigation.
Reinstates the company's oyster farming permits at Point Reyes for at least 10 years and blocks conversion of Drakes Estero to wilderness.

industries.industry: Alaska Native corporations (Kaktovik Inupiat and Arctic Slope Regional)
industries.note: Directs the Secretary to convey specified surface and subsurface land estates to these corporations, completing entitlements under prior agreements.
